subsubtopic: PRAIRIE FARM EMERGENCY FUND-CALL FOR RESIGNATION OF MINISTER-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Some 16 months have gone by since the question of the disposition of the $9,060,000 of western grain producers' PFAA contributions held in the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund was debated in this House. Despite undertakings by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), no steps have been taken to make this money available for badly needed research and development of cereal grains. The emergency fund being non-interest bearing, the Government of Canada has, in effect, stolen millions of dollars in producers' money over the years, and since the debate some 16 months ago, $1,963,000, using Farm Credit Corporation rates. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House condemn the Minister of Agriculture for having such a lack of interest in research and development and call upon the said minister to resign.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter which I sincerely hope will receive the support of all hon. members of this House. Section 37 of our new Constitution guarantees that there will be a federal-provincial conference held with native representatives within one year in order to discuss constitutional issues of concern to native people. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over a decade ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dismissed unemployment as a regrettable side effect of inflation. The situation today is more than regrettable; it is alarming. Not a day goes by that we do not learn of more firms having to reduce their work force or of going bankrupt, of more and more Canadians joining the ranks of the unemployed, and of more Canadian communities, large and small, staggering to cope with economic and social burdens. Government continues to express its indifference to the very urgent and very pressing problems of this country, problems it created through mismanagement, by citing international influences and repeatedly stating it can do nothing until other nations act. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the government stop passing what is now the devalued buck, and recognize and accept the fact that it can, indeed must, begin to implement sound economic policies, policies independent of outside conditions which would restore confidence in the business community, generate employment and get this nation back on its feet.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Several Canadian provinces have officially indicated their opposition to forced metric and have indicated that any transition ought to be purely voluntary. Public opinion polls conducted by the Metric Commission, although suppressed, show that metric is not gaining favour with the majority of the Canadian people.
The Attorney General of the province of Alberta has indicated in the Alberta legislature that his government may intervene in a court case against a Calgary woman charged with advertising carpet for sale by the square yard and by the metre using both measurements.
In the face of rising opposition and increased unpopularity, will the minister indicate whether the government is willing to consider dropping the forced aspect of metric and allowing merchants to conduct their business in the system of their choice, that is, a voluntary system?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Yesterday the CPR announced lay-offs for three weeks of 3,800 shop craft employees in Montreal, Winnipeg and Calgary. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is not bad reasoning, but we are now in a rather difficult situation. There is a slump in the export and domestic traffic of raw commodities. At the same time, grain is doing extremely well, as the hon. member and everyone should know. It is doing extremely well at this moment.

I am not blaming the companies. I realize that traffic is down and their cash flow is not very good. But surely we can follow the example of countries like Japan and France which say that we should not worry too much about today's events but plan for three, five or ten years from now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The National Harbours Board advises as follows:
1.	The National Harbours Board improved its financial performance from a net loss of $16,625,000 in 1978 to a net loss of $2,375,000 in 1979. The loss in 1979 is principally due to a strike at the port of Montreal that lasted five months and shut down the grain elevators which are major revenue generators of the corporation.
2.	As reflected in the schedule of revenue and operating income (loss), seven of the 15 ports did have an operating loss for 1979. However, in total, the National Harbours Board has a positive operating income for the first time since 1971. This reflects the results of the application of the principle of full cost recovery through tariff increases, the reduction of manpower (9 per cent in 1979), the discontinuation of non-profitable activities and the modernization of facilities (cost: $50,144,000). The benefits derived from these measures are realized to a greater extent in 1980 where the National Harbours Board had a positive operating income of $18,821,000 and a net income of $17,360,000.
3.	The ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert did show an increase in operating loss from 1978 to 1979.
(a)	This was contrary to the improvement trend established by the five other losing ports.
(b)	and (c) At the port of Churchill, the results are attributable to the lack of grain traffic. The grain volume allocated to the port is beyond the control of the National Harbours Board. Another factor was the upgrading of the port's facilities at a cost of $3,660,000 which consequently increased its depreciation and taxes by $233,000. In 1980, the operating loss is solely due to the lack of grain traffic.
At the port of Prince Rupert, the upgrading of facilities, at a cost of $1,780,000, caused depreciation expense and grants in lieu of taxes to be $183,000 higher, in total, than the previous year. However, it was an economically viable project and will earn a positive return that will more than offset the excess expenditures. The results are already showing, as evidenced by the fact that, in 1980, Prince Rupert earned $37,000 in operating income because of the project.

First, it has come to my attention that the Metric Commission is so desperate to regain its credibility and justify its very existence that it has now resorted and fallen to the temptation of escalating untruths and distortions.
I am also saddened to report that it would appear that certain ministers in the House today are of the same opinion and that, in order to keep this on track, they now find it necessary to circulate what I consider to be untruths and distortions, because the ministers who are in the House today are not saying the same thing as the minister has said over the past nine years. I will clearly document some of the statements of some of the former Liberal cabinet ministers and their position on metric.
The third concern I would like to point out, as mentioned in our motion, is that it would appear, at least to the Conservative party, that this imposition of enforced metric is creating unnecessary hardships on the business community, not to mention all of the other burdens which it has to bear at this time because of economic conditions. I will document some of those hardships.
Finally, in the summation of my remarks today, I will deal with the fallacy of the government trying to convince the Canadian people and this House of Commons that, in order to
Supply
do business in the world, it is mandatory that Canada go metric. That simply is not the case, and I will deal with that in more detail later.
First, let us deal with some of the history of metric and some of the fallacies as stated by the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in complete contradiction to the original understanding of metric. I must point out in my preamble that as opposition spokesman on the subject of weights and measures, I am not opposed to metric. I used the metric system for 25 years in business. I was a fuel oil distributor and a General Motors car dealer. I know why General Motors went metric, and I know why the fuel oil business went metric as well, I will cover that in detail later.
In commencing my remarks, I would like to refer to the statement of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on "Canada AM" just a few weeks ago. The minister said: "In general, the public has support for metric, industry supports metric and the consumers support metric." That statement was made by the same minister who, today in this House of Commons, had the nerve to say that Conservatives are trying to "brew the pot", to use his exact words.
Earlier this past month the minister also stated that this movement is motivated by a tiny group of fanatics. When we presented a petition to the House on April 6 just passed, comprising 135,327 signatures, he also had the nerve to say that that petition was the result of misleading and false representations and information. That was simply not true. If the minister were honourable, he would consider the withdrawal of that statement. Instead, as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, he made a commitment to the Canadian people, wisely or not, to respond personally and individually to each of those 135,327 signatures. I remind the minister that prior to that petition being presented, 52,000 signatures were presented to this House by myself in the same year on behalf of constituents from right across Canada. Concerning petitions presented by other Members of Parliament, as recently as this past week another 14,000 signatures came in from one area. Compounded, over 300,000 petitions have been presented to the House of Commons in less than two years.
And more to come.

These petitions have not been against metric but, rather, against forced metric. That has clearly not been the history of how we arrived at the point today where we have the implementation of the Metric Systems International. It was never intended to be forced. I will deliver some statements by three former ministers of industry, trade and commerce of the Liberal government, two ministers of small business and one minister of consumer and corporate affairs, to back up the statement that it was not to be mandatory.
I would like to refer to the minister's statement on this same TV show, "Canada AM". He said that there was a white paper, an agreement in this House in 1970, that metric should

May 14, 1982
Supply
take place. He was right, but he totally misled the people of Canada, because that agreement in 1970 was the original white paper on metric. I have it here in my hand. It was presented to this House of Commons by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the then minister of industry, trade and commerce. I refer the minister to page one of that white paper where it says:
No legislative action is contemplated which would make mandatory a general use of metric in place of inch-pound units.
The minister is misleading the Canadian public when he says that all political parties in Parliament approved the implementation in 1970 and 1971 when it approved this white paper. I will cover in more detail what the Metric Commission is saying. The minister should be fully aware of the fact that on page 10 of the same white paper, the one we all agreed to, section 4.1.7 states:
Because of the close ties between the United States and Canada in science, technology, industry and commerce, each country has a special interest in the course likely to be followed by the other in respect of metric conversion ... The question is a complex one because the United States, which is Canada's main export market, has not made the decision to convert.
Let us go on to the voluntary aspect with the agreement of the sectors involved. We are dealing now with one sector that did not agree in the beginning to move. We are dealing with weights and measures in the food industry. That is fish, meat, fruit, vegetables and other weighted-out retail products.
What did the retail sector say? I have here a copy of a letter sent to the Right Hon. Joe Clark by a major corporate manager, Patrick Carson, the corporate planning development manager for Loblaws. What did they think about it? They sat on the Metric Commission for many years. I quote from that letter to document clearly the position of that metric sector:
This letter, as you can see, is self-explanatory and for detailed information represents the wishes of approximately 85 per cent of those Canadian retailers responsible for food consumed at home.
To appreciate the efforts required to achieve this consensus statement being forwarded to Mr. Lapointe, one requires to have been exposed to the steamrolling tactics of the Metric Commission hierarchy, for a period of not less than three years.
Having objected on behalf of my particular company, for this period, to the strategy and methods imposed by the MCC it is indeed satisfying to know that the power of a government's bureaucracy is not always allowed to prevail over the wishes of its citizens-
Thank you for allowing time for this important issue to be raised on our behalf, and I am certain on behalf of many Canadians.
The letter was signed by Patrick Carson, corporate and planning development of Loblaws.
What was that consensus taken in 1981, four months before the order in council was passed by this negligent Liberal government which does not really care what the people want? Here is the consensus of the sector dealing with the implementation of metric. I quote:
The working group on scales in the retail food industry met in Vancouver on Tuesday, 28 April, 1981 and achieved the following consensus:
1. The retail food industry members of the working group wish to recommend strongly to the government that the scheduling of retail food scale
conversion to metric units in Canada, which appeared in the Canada Gazette Part 1 of 28 February, 1981, be delayed so that conversion will take place at a time closer to when retail food scales will be converted in the United States.
That is the consensus. They go on to say:
2. If the government decides to continue with the implementation of these regulations in January 1982 in spite of the above recommendations, then the retailers will continue to manage the process-
What else would they do? Corporate citizens do not intend to go to jail because they do not like the order in council. However, for this government to state over national television and at press conferences that metric is being implemented because the people want it and the sector agrees is totally untrue. There should be an apology in this House of Commons for the falsehoods and misapprehensions of this government.
I would also like to read what was said by former Liberal cabinet ministers. On March 17, 1975, Herb Gray was then minister of industry, trade and commerce. He would have people believe that ministers, government and all parties agree with metrication regardless of what the United States did. I quote Herb Gray from page 4180 of Hansard'.
-change would likely be closely related to progress in the United States toward conversion ... it may prove wise to allow the timing and process of conversion to be closely related to the development of United States practice.
That was the Liberal policy in 1975 before the government passed the order in council. The hon. member was the minister; he should have been responsible. That is what he told this House of Commons. I would now like to read a more recent answer from Hansard for April 23, 1980, given by the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe). I asked the minister this:
In light of the adverse reaction and effects to small businesses and consumers, will the minister responsible for industry, trade and commerce assure this House-and answer the question-that he will allow full parliamentary discussion on the subject of the implementation of the metric system before it is forced on business communities across Canada?
The minister replied:
If members opposite will please quiet down, Madam Speaker, I should like to tell the hon. member that the suggestion he just made will be examined.
In my supplementary question I asked:
-why must we force metrication on the people of Canada-
The minister responded:
-the government has no intention of imposing the metric system manu militari and that it has always been the policy of the Liberal party and government of taking care of the people First, not regulations.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am quite certain the hon. member is doing this inadvertently, but he is referring to ministers by name. I would ask that he refer to them by their ministry or constituency.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a statement made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. On January 14, 1981 I asked the minister:
-is it the intention of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to lock up stores, put bans around cash registers and prohibit stores from doing business-
The minister replied:
-we shall not resort to the methods the hon. member would have us use.
May 14, 1982

Those were his words, totally contrary to what he is saying today.
Let us look at a couple of other former Liberal cabinet ministers. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is infamous for referring to all-party agreement on enforced metric. The debate is not on metric but enforced metric. We are not debating the pros and cons of metric over Imperial measurement. I want to quote what was said on March 17, 1975 while introducing a motion to approve the program of guideline dates for metric conversion. The then minister of industry, trade and commerce, Alistair Gillespie, stated as reported at page 4158 of Hansard:
Every effort will be made to co-ordinate work between the two countries so as to obtain the greatest benefits for the Canadian program.
At page 4160 he stated:
Concern has also been expressed that the cost of conversion might impose an undue hardship on some small businesses.
Len Marchand, then responsible for small business, said at page 2230 of Hansard for December 21, 1976:
-the implementation dates are not mandatory, they serve as guidelines for each ... company or organization in a given sector ... The bill before us today is the first of four such bills-
We have never seen any bills in this House of Commons. We were guaranteed at that time by the minister that that was the first of four such bills before the virtual completion of the final or implementation phase of metric conversion. There are 90 acts affected and not one of those bills has ever been received in this House to this date.
The matter foremost in people's minds is, how did we get from the understanding of a voluntary approach to metric to a forced approach to metric? The Los Angeles Times figured it out. It sent someone to Canada a month ago to interview people to find out how we moved away from our understanding with the United States. Mr. Paul Robinson, ambassador of the United States to Canada, has said it would cost Canadian jobs because we cannot operate in a form of measurement foreign to the United States. I think that Mr. Robinson, the American Ambassador to Canada, is speaking the same lines Liberal cabinet ministers have spoken in this House from 1970 until today.
I have a quotation from the acting executive director of the Metric Commission, Mr. Pat Gampathy. First of all, I have this report in the Los Angeles Times for February 11, 1982:
-Canada needed to keep pace with conversion in the United States, its dominant trading partner.
Asked what his comment was, the acting executive director of the Metric Commission said:
What we do in the retail stores within Canada has no bearing on selling to the United States.
That shows me what little this acting executive director of the Metric Commission knows about retailing in border cities that rely on tourist business from the United States. He says it has no bearing, it does not matter, that we can deal in anything we want to in Niagara Falls, Ontario, regardless of what
Supply
the measurement system is in our principal tourist business with the United States. That is simply not the case. That is a lot of hogwash. There is no truth in it whatsoever.
I now refer to an article in the New York Times of March 14, 1982:
The United States ambassador, Paul H. Robinson, Jr., told Canadian reporters that metric conversion was "rubbish" and opposed by most Americans. He warned that it might create trade problems between the United States and Canada.
The Canadian Government was not pleased with Mr. Robinson's remarks since one of its basic arguments in favor of the metric system was Canada's need as a trading nation to adapt its weights and measures to the predominant system in the world.
We will find out how predominant the system is in the world in just a moment. I want now to deal with what I have currently been considering putting before the RCMP for investigation.
The minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, with all due respect, Mr. Speaker, has a conflict of interest in his position as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs responsible for the protection of the consumers of Canada against false advertising. I have risen in this House on three occasions now, going right up to three different ministers, trying to get an answer as to how come these people can do two things in the Metric Commission. They can control the media through a $1.8 million advertising tool, while at the same time spreading false rumours about how things are in Canada.
If the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has no intention of investigating articles like this full page article in The Globe and Mail, full of falsehoods and untruths, I think the RCMP should start investigating some of these statements. Statement one: "Except for retailers' scales, there is no compulsion in Canada". That is totally wrong. There are three sectors, and the minister knows it. I suggest that he bring that to the attention of the Metric Commission. Statement two: "The provinces have been a full partner in the conversion". That is not true.
What is happening in regard to the conversion program? Let us take a look at the situation with the Alberta government. I am reading from a CP story of May 13, 1982:
The Alberta government may intervene in a court case against a Calgary woman charged with advertising carpets for sale by the square yard, Attorney General Neil Crawford told the legislature Tuesday. Crawford told reporters he is not sure of all the facts. He said, however, if the charge was laid simply because the carpet company advertised in both measures, it should not be prosecuted.
Metric is not being forced, with the support of the Alberta government. Let us take a look at Manitoba's government. Let us see what is going on in their legislature, as reported by the Canadian Press on April 30, 1982:
Manitoba should tell the federal government to keep its metric snoopers out of stores in the province, Opposition Leader Sterling Lyon said Friday.
Lyon told the legislature the federal government apparently is taking legal action against carpet stores in other provinces that offer goods for sale in imperial measure as well as the metric system.

May 14, 1982
Supply
He said Attorney General Roland Penner should take the lead and advise the federal government such anti-business action would not be appreciated in Manitoba.
That does not indicate support on the part of the provincial governments. Let us move to Prince Edward Island. This is a CP story from Charlottetown, P.E.I.:
Canada's conversion to metric will be costly for this island's potato producers, says Norman Ramsay, chairman of the P.E.I. Potato Producers Association.
Legislation to enforce metric will cost producers a great deal of money to buy new scales, he said.
Ramsay also said the continued use of the Imperial System in the U.S. will aggravate the local farmers' problems.
The most serious statement of all in this full page article is a statement on the direct cost. Here is a statement by a commissioner-imagine, a commissioner. Cleo Mowers, also an editor of a western paper, obtains almost a full page story. Talk about conflict of interest! We have a metric commissioner writing an article in support of metric as an unbiased person, yet deriving his income from a stipend he receives from the minister responsible for the Metric Commission. He is spreading this kind of propaganda.
Item three: "The direct cost of forced conversion is about SI.50 per Canadian". I have not got my calculator here, but $1.50 a Canadian to me means approximately, if we have about 23 million population, a cost of $38 million or $40 million.
The minister thinks that he as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs can implement metric in the retail sectors of this country with the Metric Commission spending $50 million to date. There is $3 million for payroll, $2 million for advertising, and I do not know how much for sales promotion since they do not have to tell us what they are doing. All we know is that they have $12 million budget this year, for 12 months. They sit in an ivory tower here in Ottawa, feeding their insatiable appetite for tax dollars, the survival of the fittest, the last Metric Commission on the North American continent as of September, the last area in the free world that forced metric on people.
Even Japan has a voluntary implementation program. There is no law in Russia to prevent someone from selling a handful of beans or a pound of bananas. The point is this, that we are less free in this part of the free world than many people are in parts of the world that use the old European method. I will deal with some of those areas, in conclusion.
What does British Columbia say? Listen to one statement by the minister of education, who feels the same way as a great number of educators in different parts of the country who say that to teach only metric in our school systems is a deficiency. If we can teach French and English and graduate children out of our schools better equipped to enter the world, surely we can teach Imperial measurement in our school system, enabling those schoolchildren to deal and trade with the United States, our major trading partner which is not going to metric but going back to Imperial.
Shell Oil has just announced that in the state of Florida they are converting their pumps at considerable expense back to Imperial. So has Amoco, so has Chevron in California. Yet the
Metric Commission spreads its last piece of propaganda, that the service stations in the United States are going to metric, and that the highway signs in the United States are going to metric, both in the same article. Hogwash! I drove to Chicago and saw only one metric highway sign, by way of introduction, between Windsor and Chicago. Is that changing their highway signs? When you get to Florida you see them converting the pumps back to Imperial. If the minister thinks that is moving to metric, then he is totally out of touch. That admission indicates that he knows about as much about metric as he knows about the small business community when he says it can operate without a post office.
The RCMP investigation stems from the fact that the Metric Commission printed propaganda with the use of government presses. The commission handed that propaganda out in grocery stores and retail outlets across Canada, and that propaganda said that the Metric Commission was set up by the government in June of 1971. The Metric Commission was set up by an order in council. This governmet never passed any piece of legislation which set up the Metric Commission and gave it a mandate to bring in metric by force. As a result of a white paper we set up the Metric Commission with two main principles in mind. One was that we would change at the same time the United States changed. The second was that it would be voluntary and with the blessing of the sectors involved. 1 have proved without doubt that that is not the course that this government is on.
Hon. members on the government side have received notifications of petitions from their constituents. They have not brought those petitions into the House of Commons. They have denied their constituents the opportunity to have petitions protesting forced metric presented in this House. Is that democratic? Is that the parliamentary procedure under which we are supposed to operate? A Member of Parliament does not have to agree with a petition but, out of respect for his constituents, he should present their petitions to the House of Commons.
By going metric we are supposed to be able to do business with foreign countries. The Canadian government has just signed a contract with Japan to fill one of the largest orders even for prefabricated homes. The Japanese are moving back to Imperial and conventional two by fours. I am told the Japanese are doing this because they have to manufacture four by eights and two by fours to ship to the American market. Our Canadian metric homes are of no use to the Japanese people because a four by eight sheet of plywood will not fit a metric home, and neither will squares for roofs or blocks or bricks.
The whole world is not moving to metric. We have large orders, the most recent one to Velan Incorporated. Velan Incorporated has just received a multimillion dollar order in Montreal to supply Imperial valves to a Russian-designed
May 14, 1982

factory overseas which was Hungarian-built with Czechoslovakian participation. The order is totally in Imperial.
I have here a whole list of companies from all over the world which are ordering from Canada in Imperial. Orders in Imperal are placed with the automotive industry, the aviation industry and the aerospace industry. Orders for prefabricated homes stipulate Imperial. Orders for valves stipulate Imperial. The list is endless. And this government would have the people of Canada believe, through false advertising, that the whole world is going to metric.
Time will not permit me to list all the business that are going out of business. I see some smiles on the government side of the House. We should not be driving business out. We do not need another cross to bear. Loss of business is the cost of conversion to metric, for which there has never been proven cost justification given by this or any other government.
When the Conservatives were in office, they threw out the order in council making metric in retail stores the only form of measurement and allowed stores to do what they wanted in their sectors. In Peterborough the stores immediately went back to Imperial and now, while half of Canada is converting to metric, Peterborough is receiving cheques from the present federal government to cover the cost of their conversion back to Imperial. There are grounds for objection. People in the canning industry told this government they would not change their cans from six-ounce, ten-ounce and twelve-ounce sizes but that they would agree to put comparable metric measurements beside the Imperial measurements on the labels. They have the right idea. We do not need added costs. We do not need to exclude Imperial or Canadian measurement from use. There is no wish on the part of the Conservative opposition to bring about anything but the right to choose, when that can be justified on the basis of cost and when the sector involved requests that. The government says the majority wants forced metric. I hope sooner or later this government will come to the conclusion that it is not listening to the majority.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Oueliet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to follow the hon. member and to address this subject. The hon. member has dreamed up a cause and has devoted a lot of time and energy to trying to stop the clock. In today's world I think it is sad to see such a performance.
I believe metric should have nothing whatever to do with party politics, any more than whether motorists should be driving on the right or left side of the road and whether they should be free to choose. Metric is simply a matter of public convenience and economic necessity. Its merit has been recognized in Canadian law since 1871. In fact, it was the Tories who took the first step toward moving to metric.
Not forced.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
The first Prime Minister of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, was the first to bring in a legislative measure
Supply
dealing with metrication. He would be turning in his grave if he could listen to the hon. member speaking today.
I understand that the vast majority of the members of the hon. member's party are away today doing more important things. There are only a few left to discuss this lost cause.
In the modern world today I think one has to be dumb to oppose metrication. Metric has been requested by scientific Canadians, industrial Canadians, businessmen and consumer organizations in the country. Canada's scientific, industrial and trading communities appreciate the advantages of metric, and more and more pressure for its increased use has developed. I think former Prime Minister Diefenbaker reacted favourably to the movement to metric when he was Prime Minister, but he did not move to metric conclusively; therefore, more pressure was brought to bear. In late 1968 and soon after a number of prominent organizations in Canada asked the government to give some leadership. I could give a list of all the associations which at the time requested the Canadian government to go metric.
Not by force.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian Pharmaceutical Association-
Not by force.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

Not by force.

Not by force.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is pretty nervous. I appreciate that he would be nervous today, but I invite him to relax. He had his time in front of the camera. He is now all shook up. I think he should relax, calm down-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: And enjoy himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
-and listen. The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has received all the documentation and information necessary for a person to understand. After listening to him today and after seeing him twist the facts, I can only conclude that he does not want to read the facts correctly, that he does not want to see the facts correctly or else he is unable to do so.
I was talking about other associations which asked the Canadian government to go metric, such as the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Home and School and Parent-Teacher Federation Inc., the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Teachers' Federation and the Canadian Construction Association, just to name a few.

May 14, 1982
Supply
These associations put pressure on the government and asked it to go metric. In late 1968 or early 1969, in response to this perceived public demand, the government commissioned a committee of senior officials to investigate the demand, need, advantage and practicability of conversion to metric. Two years later this body issued a report recommending conversion, which at the time was considered both inevitable and desirable. That report was adopted by the government and became the white paper of 1970.
The Canadian government did not convert Canada to metric; the Liberal party did not convert Canada to metric; it happened by public demand. It was done and continues to be done by the people and by business, at their request and for their benefit. The white paper was submitted to the people's elected representatives who, through their House leaders in Parliament, said clearly and unequivocally: "We agree; let's get on with it."
This also required the partipation of the provincial governments and all ten Premiers agreed that the federal plan suited their own plans to convert to metric. Signs on the highways in Canada have not been put there by the federal government; they have been put there by the provincial authorities.
If the hon. member for Peterborough does not like it, he should not go around trying to make the people of Canada believe that metric has been forced on them and that it is a plan made by the Canadian government and the Liberal party. As I understand it, there are not many Liberal provincial governments in Canada but there are metric signs in every province.
In the education system today our children are taught in metric. Does the federal government, the Liberal Party of Canada or the provincial authorities run the education system in Canada? I want to tell the hon. member for Peterborough that again he is not telling the truth when he tells the people of Canada that metric has been imposed on them by the Liberal Party of Canada and by the Canadian government. Children are taught metric in school and this is through the will, desire and understanding of the provincial governments despite what the hon. member for Peterborough says.
I want to say one other thing about the voluntary aspect of metrication, Mr. Speaker. To implement such a system in Canada requires public participation. This was obtained through some thousands of volunteers representing every sector of the Canadian economy who over the last ten years organized the details of the conversion in their own sectors.
From the outset it was planned that the conversion would be as voluntary as possible, with a minimum of compulsion, but it was acknowledged that converting to metric measurement would probably require compulsion at some point. The white paper that the hon. member who spoke before me referred to and which has been unanimously endorsed in this House anticipated the compulsory conversion of retail scales.
Read it!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member is asking me to read it. If he has not read it after having launched this type of campaign for the last year and a half, that shows quite clearly that he is not serious with his campaign.
I read it. You read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
The House debated and passed two metric bills, one in 1971 and another one in 1975. It unanimously supported the resolution to approve metric conversion programs.
When the hon. member for Peterborough and the very few who follow him try to say that Parliament never approved metrication and that it was done by order in council, they are not relating what really took place. There was a lengthy debate in Parliament and there was a request by the opposition party for a formal bill. Authority for this was given by the House of Commons in 1976 through amendments to the Weights and Measures Act which specifically authorized the cabinet, by order in council, to make only metric legal in retail trade. This House approved that bill unanimously and the Conservative party voted for it in 1976.
That a few of them do not want to remember this today and regret their vote is quite possible, but the vast majority who are still around know that this is the case. The hon. member for Peterborough was not here at that time and he can say what he wants, but when he tries to convey to the public of Canada that metrication has not been amply discussed in Parliament and has not received the sanction of legislation, he is not correct. He is dead wrong.
The experience of other countries which have recently completed conversion, such as Australia and New Zealand, is that at the retail trade level there must be compulsion. The Canadian retail food industry told the government that if its scales were to be converted this should be compulsory for all merchants; so the government, having been authorized and instructed by Parliament to do so and having been requested by the industry to do so, has complied.
To pretend today that there is compulsory metrication in Canada because of the Government of Canada is not to tell the truth. The reality is that there are only three sectors where compulsory decisions have been made. In those three cases it has been done at the request of the industry-
That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: -and for very good reasons.
That is definitely wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member does not like to hear the facts. He is showing by his constant opposition to what I am saying that he does not want to know the truth.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member will have a chance to enter the debate and make his point.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
I want to say that 102 sector committees have been quietly working on the voluntary conversion of the rest of the Canadian economy. Many have completed their work and most are nearly finished now. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that until three years ago this was truly a non-partisan, nonpolitical affair for the people, and it was surely done by the people of Canada in a very non-partisan, very practical and very intelligent way. It was perceived to have broad public support and to be in response to public demand in the best interests of the Canadian economy.
It was inevitable, and to a certain degree natural, that there would be a certain measure of public resistance. In the general election of 1979 the Progressive Conservative candidate in Peterborough, seeing some pockets of resistance there, inflamed the debate, encouraged reluctance, distorted the record, and put the whole responsibility on the Liberal government. In so doing, he was able to win a seat in Parliament for
Supply
the riding of Peterborough. Well, he might have been successful at distorting the facts in his own riding, but now he comes to Ottawa and tries to distort the facts and make a case among his colleagues. Judging by the number I see around him today, he has not been very successful in convincing many of his colleagues to support his fight.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the minister knows we have a conference today which our party members are attending. I wish he would-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: That is what I said, Mr. Speaker. The party has a convention, which is much more important. So they are there and a few dumb MPs like him are here wasting there time and using up the time of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) on a point of order.
1 would ask the minister to withdraw that remark; he called us "dumb". That is an unparliamentary expression and he should withdraw it. If there is any dumbness around here, we know where it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yes, indeed. I am sorry, I want to withdraw. I am talking about the hon. member for Peterborough who thinks it is more appropriate to waste his time here than to go to the national convention of his party.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Peterborough on a point of order.
If he is referring to the hon. member for Peterborough, as he says, then I would ask him to withdraw the word "dumb".

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: If it bothers the hon. member, I indeed appreciate his sensitivities; but I think it is unfortunate that an hon. member would think it is more important to attack a program which was implemented in Canada for the good of our country and which will bring much more value to our commercial activities that to go to his own party convention. I regret that he finds his time is spent more usefully in this House today than with the numerous other members of his party now having their convention.
Sad, sad.
Nothing better to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The reasons we moved to metric in Canada are numerous and the benefits of metric conversion are well known. However, I would like to put them on record because obviously the hon. member has not seen them. Metric saves classroom time. Training in metric creates Canadian jobs.

For civil servants.

May 14, 1982
Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Metric means fewer package sizes for consumers. Metric makes shopping easier and it simplifies calculations. Metric eases international communications. These are six fundamental reasons why we moved to metric in Canada.
You are unbelievable.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The exclusive use of the metric system in our schools simplifies the teaching of mathematics and many of the natural sciences. This has resulted in an estimated saving of 5 per cent to 10 per cent in the time it takes to teach the school curriculum. This time can be and is being used to teach more useful things than the number of feet in a mile or yards in a furlong. Secondly, trading in metric creates Canadian jobs.
Who wrote that?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Canada needs to produce goods in metric to trade with a predominantly metric world.
The United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Our standard of living depends on our export trade. Over 31 per cent of every Canadian dollar is earned from exports, versus less than 6 per cent to the United States. Producing cars and parts in metric for the United States by itself is keeping over 100,000 Canadians employed. With our newsprint, wood pulp, petroleum and natural gas industries also converted to metric, close to 50 per cent of our exports, even to the U.S., are now described in metric units.
The idea put forward by the opposition that we should not convert to metric because the Americans are not converting is totally false, Mr. Speaker. The vast majority of American industry doing business with Canada and throughout the world is already totally metric. These American companies who have subsidiaries in Canada have brought metric to Canada through those subsidiaries. Therefore, this argument that we should not go metric because the Americans are supposedly slowing down their conversion is totally wrong.
When we resume at two o'clock 1 will continue on this subject-
Oh, no!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: -and read a letter from President Ronald Reagan on this subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock.

speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
When the House adjourned at one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was saying, quite contrary to what was said by the hon. member opposite, that President Reagan in the United States is supporting the effort to go metric. He wrote a letter dated April 6, 1982 to members of the American National Metric Council on the occasion of their eight annual conference. He wrote:
My administration supports the policy of voluntary metrication expressed in the Metric Conversion Act of 1975.
Voluntary?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The Conservatives are excited because the letter mentioned voluntary metrication. Voluntary metrication is what we have in Canada.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
The President's letter continues:
As the representative of the private sector in this area, your council fulfils an important role in facilitating such conversion. I look forward to continued cooperation with your organization as we work together to make the United States more competitive in world markets.
If it is good enough for the United States, it is indeed good for Canada. What we are trying to do is to be more competitive in the world markets. This is one of the reasons we are going metric.
I want to return to two aspects which were developed by the opposition. One has to do with the impression that we are imposing metrification, making it compulsory and not voluntary. More than 100 sectors of the industry are operating voluntarily within the framework of the mandate of the white paper on metrication.
There have been only three area where regulation have been passed making metrication compulsory. In these three cases the passive of regulations was done at the insistence and request of the industry. The first one has to do with gasoline sales by the litre. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that it was at the request of the gasoline industry that appropriate regulations were passed to make the sale of gasoline by the litre mandatory.
Blackmail.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: The second area is that of home furnishings. The third one is the retail food scale sector. In these two cases regulations were passed clearly at the request of the industry-
That's nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
-and at the request of consumer associations in Canada. Why was that done? It was done for a very simple reason. It was felt that to do otherwise would create confusion and difficulties. As well, it would not have been in the best
May 14, 1982

interests of the consumer. The industry stated that if appropriate regulations were not passed in the area of home furnishings and that of retail food scales, it would be incorrect and unjust for many retailers or clients.
The special committee of the home furnishings industry requested, after unanimous approval by all the various national associations that were involved in this special committee, that regulations be passed to make sure that metric conversion would take place in all areas at the same time. This decision was based on the reasonable assumption that someone buying carpeting would likely be wanting to look at furniture, bedspreads, wallpaper and other similar types of products.
It was also felt that, because of the competitive nature of their own industry, regulations would be required to ensure that all retailers converted at the same time. If this is true for the home furnishing sector, it is equally true for retail food scales. If this did not occur, the consumer would be unable to compare prices easily between stores where one might show the price per square yard while another may show the price per square metre, which is approximately 20 per cent larger.
In the motion which is before us today, the opposition would like us to stop the prosecutions which have come before the courts in relation to the implementation of the regulations dealing with home furnishings. Once again the hon. member for Peterborough is misleading the House when he quotes me as saying that I assured him that there would be no prosecutions against those who are faced today with the implementation of metric retail food scales. In fact, it is very clear that the implementation of the retail food scale conversion program will take place over two years and we are confident that by the end of that two-year period-that is, by the end of next year- everyone would have complied with the regulations and there would be no reason to prosecute.
The hon. member mentioned some prosecutions which he read about in the newspapers. I do not want to comment on those cases but I do want to say to him that to abandon prosecutions at the present time would be unfair to those who were involved for a number of years in the implementation of the regulations concerning home furnishing. If prosecutions have taken place in that regard, it was indeed at the request of the Canadian Carpet Institute and at the request of those who have said that it is not fair to advertise a product at a price which is obviously lower than the price advertised under the metric measure. Therefore, in fairness to all the retailers in the industry, allowing some retailers to advertise a price to consumers under one system that is different from the price using the metric system could give undue advantage to some retailers. It is precisely for this reason that the industry itself has requested that the appropriate regulations come into place.
With respect to those who are peacefully converting their retail food scales in an orderly fashion, according to the plan which was asked for and designed by the industry itself with
Supply
the support of the Consumers' Association of Canada, we will indeed be helping them to facilitate this conversion. We will co-operate with them in order to facilitate this conversion and make sure that it is done in an orderly fashion.
I disagree with the motion that has been presented today which alleges that the enforcement of metrication is causing substantial hardship and contributing to an increasing rate of bankruptcies. I suggest that this is grossly misleading. I know of no case where a retailer who has been asked to change his scales has been forced into bankruptcy because of the cost of the new scales. Some opposition members have gone to see retailers contending that it will cost thousands of dollars to change their scales. This is not true. For a few hundred dollars new scales can be purchased or converted. I repeat that you can have scales converted to metric for just a few hundred dollars. Retailers have two years to accomplish this.
the government is not imposing this program. It is following the views and advice of the industry, and it is only at the request of the industry that regulations were passed. As I indicated earlier in my speech, these regulations were authorized by Parliament, by legislation tabled in Parliament and approved unanimously by Parliament.
In the spirit of co-operation I am prepared to discuss with the people involved in this sector in the coming weeks the possibility of exempting some small retailers from compulsory metrication. It is common knowledge that when we implemented the regulations for sale of gasoline by the litre, we exempted some retailers marketing diesel fuel who did not exceed a particular amount of sales. I believe this could be contemplated in relation to those concerned with retail food scales.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. minister but his allotted time has expired.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: I just have a closing statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This can be done with the unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: I thank hon. members for allowing me to finish because I do want to make an important point which I think they want to know. In this regard, the government has never acted unilaterally to impose regulations or force compulsory metrication. The only exeptions-the three I have mentioned-out of the 100 sector industries which are going metric in Canada result from regulations which were passed at the specific request of the industry.
No, that is not right.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
1 am therefore ready to have discussions with these people to find out if it is feasible to excuse some small retailers from compulsory metrication. If the industry agrees with this and allows us to do it, I will indeed come forward and announce it. I do not think it would be fair or correct for the government to do this unilaterally.

May 14, 1982
Supply
The Consumers Association of Canada and the various retail council associations of Canada have requested compulsory regulations in this regard. Therefore, before doing anything I want to consult with them to discuss the implications.
In closing, I want to say that we in the government, and I believe the vast majority of Canadians, believe the pace, the degree and the nature of change to the metric system should, and must, be determined voluntarily in the various sectors of trade and industry by the individual firms or industries directly concerned, with minimal government interference. I took that last remark directly from a speech which was made by my hon. friend opposite. I share his view in that regard.
We do not want to impose metrication on anyone. We believe that the vast majority of Canadians want it because they believe it is in the best interests of Canada. However, we also understand and appreciate that in order for it to be implemented fairly and in an orderly fashion, some regulations must be passed to protect the majority against the unacceptable competition of a minority. In these cases, particularly in the retail sector, it is important that we protect the large majority of those who want to accept metrication. They are welcoming this opportunity because they know that through metric we have substantially reduced and rationalized the number of package sizes and that we have been able to standardize them using round metric sizes to the best advantage of consumers. Those in the industries who have voluntarily accepted this must be protected against the few exceptions who will not follow the rule and who could try to take undue and unfair advantage in the marketplace. This is why some regulations were passed, and it is why we have some regulations, at the request of the industries, I repeat again.
The motion which is presented to us today unfortunately sides more with the past than with the future. I think it is a regressive resolution. It is not a resolution which is in the best spirit of Canada, a young nation looking to the future, looking for markets abroad, looking for opportunities. I think the motion presented by the hon. member for Peterborough should be massively rejected.

Mr. Speaker, this issue was presented to all members of Parliament in my first year here, in 1968, in 1969 and again in 1970. The series of events which have occurred since 1969 include the presenting of a white paper on metric conversion in 1970, amendments to the Weights and Measures Act (1971), a motion to approve the program of guidelines for metric conversion in 1975, Bill C-23, Metric Conversion (Statute Law Amendment, 1976) Act, from December 1976 until June of 1977, and a no-confidence motion in June of 1980. That was the series of parliamentary events which occurred. Mixed in with those were numerous hearings in two or three committees of this House.
The motion of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) carefully avoids stating that the Conservatives were opposed to conversion to a metric system of measurement in
Canada. I am glad that it was carefully avoided. In fact, the hon. gentleman carefully avoided saying that in his speech.
The first studies launched with regard to conversion to metric in Canada took place under the Diefenbaker administration in 1960, 1961 and 1962. Finally, a white paper evolved through the channels of the bureaucracy in this capital and it was presented to Parliament. We held hearings. I will deal with some of the activities of the minister a little later.
The minister mentioned a number of organizations which supported the conversion to metric, but I also want to add to that list some more independent witnesses who testified in relation to Bill C-23 in 1977. We heard the testimony of Mr. Lister, chairman of the Metric Advisory Committee, although what he said might not carry too much weight. We heard from Mr. Gilbey, of the grain services union. We heard from Mr. Dobson Lee, president of Alberta Unifarm, who said, "We have supported the metric system for a good many years." We heard from Mr. A. E. Hall, president of the Manitoba Farm Bureau, Mr. Eyre, director of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, and Mr. Hart of the Saskatchewan urban municipalities, who said: "We accept a program of conversion to metric." Of course, we also heard from Mr. Maine, who was then vice-president of the National Farmers Union. All of these various organizations appeared before parliamentary committees. I was there to hear them.
The question is not what is being done but, rather, how it is being done. I gather that no one in the official opposition will stand up-certainly the hon. member for Peterborough did not-and outrightly oppose the conversion of Canada's measurement system to the metric system. The Conservatives will not do that. Therefore, the question is not what but, rather, how.
Emphasize that.

I have problems concerning the kind of eighteenth or seventeenth century propaganda and baloney which has been put out in the country by various and sundry people in the Conservative party, which has been nothing more than a sheer scare campaign. It is the old turn-the-clock-back syndrome, but we cannot turn it back. Every organization has said, "Whether we like metric or not, we cannot stop it and we cannot turn it back." The country elevator systems for grain handling in the prairie provinces have already gone through a few million dollars converting to metric scales. I do not imagine anyone in this House who would want to junk it, throw it out and go back to something else. Almost every private enterprise organization has already converted. In fact, 65 per cent of the B.C. forest industry has already converted and there is no way it can turn back.
Let me return to the question not of what we are doing but, rather, how we are doing it. We do not need any neanderthal organization which is in opposition to metric. I challenge any hon. member in this place to interrupt me on a point of order if the hon. member is opposed to bringing about conversion to the metric system in Canada. I challenge any hon. member of
May 14, 1982

this House to get up right now and tell me, on a point of order, that the hon. member is opposed to conversion to metric.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Not one.
I do not hear a word, Mr. Speaker.
I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Red Deer rises on a point of order.
Could the hon. member tell us to which system of metric he is referring? Then we would probably know. Which one of the four or five systems is he talking about?

Mr. Speaker, I could read a couple of quotes of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) if he wants me to embarrass him. The hon. member for Red Deer realizes that the system of metric conversion being used is under the rules and regulations of the Parliament of Canada. That is the system of metric we are referring to.
That is nonsense.
You do not know what you are talking about, Les.
Mr. Speaker, I am just as far behind as the hon. member for Red Deer with regard to conversion. I am just as far behind, too, because-
You can say that again.
-I have not caught up with it yet, and that is probably the problem of the people of Canada. So nobody, but nobody, in this House opposes Canada converting to the metric system of measurement.
On a voluntary basis.
Let us get to the question concerning not what the government is doing but, rather, how it is doing it. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) mentioned that it should be on a voluntary basis.
Right.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that is some kind of Saturday night beer parlour dreaming. General Motors, for example, has already converted to metric, and a farmer in the hon. member's riding who buys a GM car or truck does not have a choice. It is not voluntary for him. He is into metric whether he likes it or not. It is not a case of compulsion or voluntariness; rather, it is a case of attrition and habit. That is not necessarily criminal. Some habits happen to be good.
The minister and the government have been less than reasonable in terms of how the costs of conversion are being shared among the population of Canada. That is the main complaint. A farmer purchases a pail of chemicals. It is measured in litres, but his sprayer is calibrated for Imperial gallons. The chemical industry lobbied the government to have
Supply
this chemical measured only in litres and the government agreed. There is no reason why there cannot be two sets of directions on the label for both litres and gallons. The farmer cannot be expected to throw out his sprayer and buy a new one.
The matter of dual directions is similar to dual languages. The minister has been a bit supine with regard to statements by various and sundry multinational corporations designed to make it cheaper and more convenient for them. I invite the minister to launch an investigation into how multinational corporations which manufacture scales are hitting our retail merchants and garage men on the head with the prices they charge. It is outrageous.
Members on all sides of the House have merchants in their constituencies who have been taken advantage of when converting to the new scales. If the minister wants conversion to metric to be more acceptable and agreeable to the ordinary citizens of this country, whether they be small-business men or farmers, that is where he should move. It is not necesary to fine anyone. Metric conversion is irrevocable; it is here whether we like it or not. I gather we all like, but do not understand all of it.
I again say to the minister it is not what we are doing, but how we are doing it. That is the problem which is causing the neanderthal and eighteenth century reactions in places like Peterborough.
I understand that the 50 per cent write-off for the plumber, electrician, pipefitter or tinsmith when buying a new set of tools expired on March 31, but that the minister has now agreed to extend that. I hope he will nod his head if I am correct. I hear some rattling from over there. Is it correct that he has extended the provision beyond March 31 so that this 50 per cent write-off will still apply?
I further understand the extension will be covered by a new set of regulations. 1 hope whatever member on the government side speaks, the minister will provide him with the material to tell us what these new regulations will be. There has not been a word of objection from any of the three parties with regard to metric conversion. What the government is doing is okay. How it is being done is the problem.
The cost of conversion should be borne by the nation as a whole. There should just not be a 50 per cent benefit for the mechanic who has to buy a new set of tools or the small storekeeper who has to buy a new scale. There should be a 100 per cent write-off immediately. If the government wants a greater degree of acceptance, support and speed in the conversion to metric, those are the kinds of things it must do. This is something the country should do together, all of us.
I object to the mindless baloney put out by various and sundry people, those people mainly to my right and their mindless opposition to any kind of change. Every organization which appeared before this and previous Parliaments back to 1970 said to convert. The nicest quote of all is one from a good

May 14, 1982
Supply
friend, a gentleman I admire. This was said in 1975 when we were debating Bill C-23. The hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) was the lead-off speaker. He said:
-we supported metric conversion when it was introduced by order in council and the white paper, and that is our position today-we still support it, but we have reservations and hope to place them on the record during this debate.
That is what he and a number of his colleagues then proceeded to do. He went on to say:
Metric conversion in Canada will put us in step with the rest of the world.
He said that his party was "appalled at the lack of progress being made" by the Metric Commission. One of the most respected members ever in this House, the former member for Peace River, Mr. Baldwin, in 1970 completely supported the opening statement by the minister in the white paper on metric conversion. The former member for Malpeque who went on to become Premier of Prince Edward Island had a private members' bill to implement metrication. I do not think the hon. member for Peterborough really believes there should not be a conversion to metric.
The costs of conversion for every plumber, electrician, mechanic, pipefitter, retail merchant, tool and dye maker or whatever, should be recoverable through the tax system by a tax credit, tax exemption, 100 per cent write-off or grant. I do not care how it is done. When someone has to put out $5,000 or $6,000 for a scale for a corner grocery store, the merchant does not necessarily object about the conversion to metric but to the fact that he has to pick up at least half the tab. That is not fair. I therefore urge the minister to be generous in the regulations he brings forward.
I am glad he has extended the period beyond March 31. He should now look at other sectors of the economy to which that extension should apply and provide a 100 per cent recovery of the actual cost. All people have to do is attach their receipts to their income tax form. If the government wants more cooperation and support with regard to metric conversion, that is the only decent thing to do.
It took almost 50 years for Canada to go metric in our monetary system. It took us almost 50 years to go from pounds, shillings and pence to dollars and cents. I hope to goodness it will not take us that long to do the same thing with metric measurements in other parts of our economy. In fact, I find it ironic and amusing that in 1871 Sir John A. Macdonald had legislation passed in this place that made both Imperial and metric legal. The Conservatives were unanimous in their support of it, and the Liberals opposed it. Believe it or not, they opposed it!
Another reason seems to be that neither one has a policy. I am glad the Conservatives are going to Toronto; I hope they come up with a policy for a change. I urge the eight or nine of them who are here, as soon as the House adjourns, to head for
Toronto and come up with a policy on metric-or on anything else.
Oh, oh!
You guys should not laugh.
Tell them about their policy.
This government is the outfit, Mr. Speaker, that says they are not left-wing or right-wing but middle of the road.
Bang in the centre.
And that is where all the accidents happen.
Hear, hear!

They try to please everybody and end up pleasing nobody. They have got the whole country mad at them, whether it is on interest rates or metric conversion or whatever. I do not mind a fellow being dumb if he cannot help it; it is when they work at it. That is what bothers me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. He may continue if there is unanimous consent.
Agreed.
I want to thank the House and appreciate their courtesy. Under the rules, I can go to five o'clock!
Hear, hear!
I promise my colleagues I will not do that. In fact, my own colleagues are asking me not to do that.
That would be worse than the bells for two weeks.

In the course of a change to a fundamental apparatus in the operation of a society and its economy, and in the course of having measurements for the goods we produce and sell, every civilization, every population, adapts and then changes. The whole history of this problem, which goes back thousands of years, has been one of the entire world trying to get one common system-
Hear, hear!

-one system which, no matter where you are in this world, no matter what language you speak, no matter what kind of political regime you are under, would mean a common communication between men, among mankind.
Social democracy.
While there are problems, while there are people who do not want change, they are a minute number of the total population.
Right on!

There are those problems that automatically come about when you make a significant major change. What
May 14, 1982

else is new? One of the British kings said that a foot is as long as his foot and a yard is as long as his arm. They had a great deal of problems about that kind of change.
Oh, oh!

The kind of help 1 am getting, Mr. Speaker, from behind me is not much help!
It seems to me that it is incumbent on all parties to assist, in every way we can, our fellow citizens in adapting and converting to this change. That is an obligation we all have, since all of us supported the conversion to metric. But the other obligation falls upon the government. You do not need to fine anybody. Any merchant who decides voluntarily not to convert to metric is going to go broke three or four years down the road; he will be out of business. His suppliers will not understand his orders because those orders will be in Imperial measure and he will not get his supply. His customers will understand kilograms and litres and they will not understand his pints and pounds. So you do not need any fines. In fact, Mr. Speaker, all 282 of us could rally a wealth of support and effort to understand. I suspect that I, among many other members of this House, am still in my head about 10 or 15 years behind in this conversion matter. My children know it. I do not have any grandchildren but the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) has grandchildren who understand it. It is there; it is a fact of life; it is a reality. This mindless screaming and yelling really harms the country. All we need is to get the government to be a little smarter about how they are doing it, not what they are doing.
Its tough on the Liberals.

I urge the minister to go to his colleague, that tightwad, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), and the other tightwad, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and get 100 per cent credit on the cost of conversion to metric. That will help a lot of ordinary citizens.
The corporations have already converted and have passed on the cost to the customers. In the price of your car, tractor or combine, those costs have been passed on. The consumers are absorbing them. But the corner grocer, the plumber, the people who are still converting, buying another set of tools or a new set of scales, do not have sufficient benefit. They are not being treated equally under our tax laws or under our pricing system. The corporations have already done the conversion, many of whom persuaded the government to do the conversion. The minister should be very generous in this conversion and forget about taking people to court and having fines imposed.
Hear, hear!

Anyone who will not convert now will convert in any event four or five years from now. That will not be because it is compulsory, not because it is not voluntary, but just because he will not have any choice. It will have become the mode used in our economy and in our commerce. We have probably got more than halfway to completion already. You cannot fly in the face of what is actually going on and expanding.
Supply
In regard to the United States, I recall that in a committee in 1970 and in this House, and again in 1971 and again in 1975, we were told the Americans were going to convert and that we were going to convert in Canada within ten years. Well, it is taking us 12 or 15 years. It will take the Americans 20 or 25 years, but the Americans are going to convert; there are no ifs, ands or buts. It is likely that it will not be done by the American government but by the multinational corporations. They are going to make sure that the American bolt fits in a French tank. That is already in process. The Standing Committee on Transport visited Bombardier, which manufactures LRC trains. Bombardier was the successful tenderer in New Jersey, Oregon, Washington, California and various cities.
And Mexico.

Mexico and various cities and states in the United States. When those states and cities called for tenders, they asked for them in metric; they did not ask for them in inches, yards or pounds. The process in corporations and state and municipal governments in the United States is already in place, regardless of what the Ronald Reagan republicans have to say. It is already in place. It is there. It will grow. It will take five or ten years longer in the United States than it will here, but that is the only difference.
I agree with the gist of the motion of the hon. member for Peterborough as it applies to how the government is implementing metrication. I hope we have persuaded the minister that it is the "how" that is important. I hope he will go back to the drawing board and be much more generous with the people metric costs.
A farmer puts so many bushels of wheat and so many gallons of treatment for his seed into his drill. In his sprayer he puts in so many pounds of chemicals or fertilizers. There is one thing which could be made compulsory tomorrow, and there is no darned reason in the world why the minister should not do it. We would agree that it should be compulsory that chemical companies put dual directions on five-gallon cans or on bulk tanks which are delivered by various and sundry fertilizer, petroleum and insecticide distributors. That would help people understand and convert, and it would save them time and money. That is the proper route.
While we support the gist of the motion of the official opposition, we dislike the direction some hon. members of the official opposition have taken. At the same time we dislike the methods used in implementing conversion to metric, particularly as they apply to tradesmen, retail merchants and farmers. This is the area in which the minister must be much more generous.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin)
was-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Chair recognized a Liberal speaker and then an NDP speaker, and now the Chair is recognizing another Liberal speaker. This is our opposition day.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I understand the concern of the hon. member very well, but it has always been a practice, accepted by the whips of the parties-with whom the Chair co-operates on a continual basis-that we alternate from a government spokesman to an opposition spokesman.
