You will be next, Gordon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
You have not heard the last of this one, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am rising for the third time, Mr. Speaker. The opposition keeps objecting, as it is doing with respect to the metric system. Hon. members opposite are heading headlong into the eighteenth century and moving the clock back. Even a stopped clock is right twice every 24 hours.
I was not here in the House when metric was passed and I was not here when it began to be implemented, but I was a citizen and I remember the initial reaction at the border when a CBC reporter interviewed Americans coming over to Canada. One person was asked what he thought of Celsius. He said, "I haven't even been there yet." Then the interviewer asked another person whether he thought the change would make much difference in the distance between Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury. That person said, "I think so; it will be a shorter trip." This story is part of the historical record, and it should be on the record because this is a very serious debate this afternoon. The reporter tried to correct that person. He said that the distance between the cities would not change. He said it was the same distance. The American replied, "Yes, but the kilometres go by faster!"
I have since learned that there have been other benefits. I checked with my secretary, and she tells me that it is psychologically good for a woman to go into a store and say: "I wear a size 92 centimetre". My secretary also tells me the metric system is good because people are now only half their previous weight!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: That is why Kempling supports it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am told that is why the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) supports it. There is a psychological benefit.
Usually I say it is a pleasure and a privilege to speak here on a Friday afternoon, but today is historic. The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) was elected in 1979 on an antimetric platform. He defeated the Hon. Hugh Faulkner. The hon. member for Peterborough waited so long for his metric ship to come in that his pier collapsed. Where is he? He has left the House. His pier has collapsed. Until I did some research last night I did not understand why the only questions he has asked in the House and the only motions he has moved in the House over the last three years have been about the metric system.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There have been other questions?
Of course.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I stand corrected, but when I have been here the only questions put and the only motions moved by the hon. member for Peterborough have been about the metric system.
He asked about capital punishment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, he asked about capital punishment. I am sorry. I stand corrected by the hon. member opposite.
The hon. member for Peterborough must understand history. I have researched it. The hon. member keeps talking about the Imperial system. What he does not realize is that the Imperial system he wants to adopt is really a French system. The French got rid of it at the time of the revolution when they went metric, followed by about 90 per cent of the world. I know a lot of history about this subject because I was very serious in preparing for today's debate. The crazy 60s cycle we are in is from Babylon. It is a mystical, religious thing. There are 60 seconds, 360 degrees and 60 minutes. Feet come from paces. If a room was 20 paces by 30 paces, the measurement evolved to be 20 feet by 30 feet.
There is a big difference between the origin of the Roman or Italian inch and the English inch. The inch actually comes from the Roman uncia, which means one-twelfth of anything. The English came along and said, "No, no; historically the inch comes from three barley corns." The English said that three barley corns equal one inch. As a matter of fact, even today barley corns are used in shoes. The difference between a shoe size nine and a shoe size ten is one barley corn, or one-third of an inch.
The matter gets more complicated when we get to miles. The mile comes from the Italian milliare, which was the distance a Roman army would cover if it marched 1,000 paces. A mile was 5,000 Roman feet. The English would have nothing to do with that. One could not divide English feet and yards into the Roman mile, so the English came up with the statute mile. This expression is borrowed from the Italian word
May 14, 1982

statutum, or "that which is set up". Why? Because it would not divide.
It was not good enough for the English just to have statute miles because the English had their navy to consider. The navy did not want to go with the statute mile, so it went with the nautical mile. A nautical mile is 6,076.1 feet. If that were not bad enough, the English had to have a third mile, the admiralty mile, which is 6,080 feet. That is what we have to live with today. As a matter of fact, around my area of Sault Ste. Marie, between what has been done in England and what has been done in the United States, we now have three types of pints, two types of quarts and three types of gallons. We have a system of pints, quarts and gallons that is different from pints, quarts and gallons in Sault, Michigan. The United States also has another system of pints and gallons, so we wind up with three types of pints, three types of gallons and two types of quarts. That is what we are trying to rationalize.
There is nothing new about all this, Mr. Speaker. It goes back as far as the French Revolution. In 1789 the French got rid of the system that we are trying to evolve from, and by 1840 they had the metric system. I do not think things would have changed in Canada had it not been for the imperial push we received in 1965 when, because of the demands of industry, the United Kingdom decided to go metric. The big impetus for this whole program came from the United Kingdom. It was not only Canada that was affected either. In 1968 South Africa, Ireland, Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda were affected; in 1969 New Zealand and Rhodesia adopted the system. As a matter of fact, in New Zealand everything is metric at the moment except for snooker and billiards. In 1970 Canada, Sri Lanka and Zambia began the changeover.
All the countries in the world except Canada, the U.S.A., the United Kingdom, South Yemen, Burma, Brunei and Borneo are now either operating in metric or very close to it.
The history of what has happened in Canada has been told several times but it bears repeating. It is not something new. We have had the two systems in Canada since 1871. As a matter of fact, they have had the two systems in the United States almost as long. In 1875 we signed the Treaty of Metre; in 1960 the Agreement of Metric Nations and then in 1970 there was the white paper on metric conversion.
Who has supported all this, Mr. Speaker? The list represents a cross-section of the country. There is the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Hospital Association, the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canadian Construction Association, and the Canadian Teachers' Federation. The white paper of January 16, 1970, was supported by Mr. Ged Baldwin of the Progressive Conservative Party, the hon. member for Winnipeg-North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the NDP, and Mr. Gilbert Rondeau for the Social Credit Party. All three parties agreed with the white paper.
On March 17, 1975, when the guideline dates were moved in the House they were supported by the hon. member for
Supply
Burlington (Mr. Kempling) for the Progressive Conservative Party, Mr. Arnold Peters for the NDP and Mr. C. A. Gauthier for the Social Credit Party.
In 1976 the omnibus bill went from the House to the committee, witnesses were heard, it came back and-as far as history will ever record it-was passed unanimously by the House. I am surprised that after all these years the hon. member does not know what a vote in the House is. The bill was voted on and passed. If the hon. member opposite did not like it then, he should have stood up and at least have been on record as opposing it.
It was not voted on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was a vote of the House in 1976. In 1971 the provinces unanimously supported the resolution, and in 1977 they changed their highway signs. It is now in all provincial school curricula, and on all highway signs. Each province has a metric co-ordinator. The national building code is in metric. New Brunswick was the first province to adopt it in October, 1981.
Let us look at what happened in the business sector. The Ford Motor Company has build the Escort, the Lynx and LN7 according to metric specifications. The company says that within three to five years it will convert its operation completely to metric. General Motors began its conversion in 1973, and at the moment 95 per cent of its car output is in metric.
Mr. Ray Pinard, chairman of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, says that they " .. . have been shipping to overseas markets for years in metric."
The output of steel is now 20 per cent metric. The food industry is 70 per cent metric. Ellis-Don Ltd. of Toronto says that 40 per cent of its projects are completely metric.
We should consider the costs now, Mr. Speaker. General Motors says that it amounts to less than one per cent of the cost estimates made in 1960. Mr. Bill Ellison, director of engineering standards for General Motors says that it was "easier than we anticipated". Mr. Ron Strang, supervisor of engineering standards for Caterpillar Tractor Company says, "It hasn't been difficult at all." He also says that "I think everyone has made a mountain out of this thing".
The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) is so lost for issues that he comes here making a mountain out of a molehill. I cannot think of a greater waste of the taxpayers' money on a Friday afternoon. I am not sure of the cost of keeping the House of Commons open, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is about $500,000 per day. I cannot think of a worse use of the taxpayers' money than to spend $500,000 on this issue today. We have economic problems and more important things to do in the country. I think this is a waste of the taxpayers' money, and I want that on record.
The hon. member for Peterborough is always talking about what is happening in the United States. Of the top 1,000 manufacturing and industrial firms in the United States, two thirds foresee using metric as their predominant system. Most of them make at least one product in metric and more than

May 14, 1982
Supply
half favour metric conversion within the next 20 years. Only 16 per cent report sales losses due to lack of supply of metric sizes. School children are learning the system in the United States; cameras are metric; film is metric; prescription drugs are metric; ski equipment is metric. In electricity supplies, amperes, volts and watts are all metric. Soft drinks, wines and alcoholic beverages are metric, so are grocery stores; General Motors will be fully metric this year, and 20 per cent of gas pumps will have converted to metric.
The Port of New Orleans handles 18 per cent of offshore transportation and it wants a total conversion to metric in order to protect foreign markets. The fastener industry in the United States plans total conversion. The food and drug administration wants the nutrition data in metric on all food packages. President Reagan supports the 1975 act, contrary to what is said by hon. members opposite.
It comes down to a choice of whether we make metric mandatory at certain times. Japan did not, and it took that country 40 years to convert. England started the program, then got cold feet and now there is chaos because it is half in and half out. Australia started at the same time we did and has completed the program. Mr. John Norgard, the head of the Australia Metric Conversion Board has said that the most trouble-free changeovers were those in which it was possible to have a definite cut-off.
There are several reasons why we should be moving to metric, Mr. Speaker, the most important of which is that 90 per cent of other nations in the world have converted. Mr. Cleo Mowers of the Metric Commission has said that two systems will not work; that the United States is going metric; that the provinces are full partners; that at all times there has been allparty support for the program; that in a few years most Canadians will know only the metric system, and that other nations have gone through the same process and have no regrets.
In this House when a whip or a leader speaks for his party, that should be accepted as the position of that party. I do not think we can push and pull in politics, at least not in the House of Commons, and retain credibility.
On November 14, 1979 when this party was in opposition, the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Chenier) put this question to the then minister for consumer and corporate affairs:
-I would like to ask the minister how he intends to ensure that metric conversion is completed, or does he intend to act on his own to dismantle the program?
The minister said:
Certainly not, Mr. Speaker. The government-
Which was Progressive Conservative at the time:
-is still wedded to the concept of metrication.
But not forced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The world moves on-
The Tories don't.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Tories do not. That is exactly where I was heading. The Tories move onward to the 18th century. That has been their history on the NEP, the budget, the Charter of Rights; you name it. I have been sitting here for two years, not debating the future but debating and listening to the past. It is no different today. The Tories move on with vigour and passion into the 18th century. But with or without them it will move.
It is difficult to change the status quo, but the responsible thing to do for Canada and Canadians is to move with the times. This we have done, Mr. Speaker, patiently and within the process we know, and that is exactly what history will record. In the final analysis I think this whole process will be nothing but a footnote, because we are going to be virtually the last country on this planet to convert to the metric system.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I reserve the right to bring up a question of privilege on the Speaker's decision whether it was my turn to speak. We had a speaker, the government side had a speaker, and the NDP had a speaker on our motion. I felt I was entitled to be the next speaker, but the Speaker chose a member from the government side. In other words, they had two back to back.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Not back to back.

I am not going to waste the time of the House arguing about it; we will do that another time. However, I have never heard so much garbage in all my life as I have today from the minister and his parliamentary secretary, as well as the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). Talk about people who do not know what they are talking about!
Mr. Speaker, I just want to correct a statement made by the hon. member. The government side did not have speakers back to back as he just stated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) has made his point. I am sure the matter will be examined and if there are further discussions they will take place at an appropriate time.

Mr. Speaker, as to the hon. member for Regina West, I have never seen a case of skinned shins like the one he displayed today because there is not way a person can come down on both sides of the fence without getting skinned. Of course a person who tries to sit on the fence and keep his ear to the ground gets out of position, and I guess that is what has happened to the hon. member today. I ask the hon. member for Regina West what form of metric was he talking about. There are so many different types of measurements in the world today that it is creating horrendous problems, especially for the agriculture industry. The minister and his parliamentary secretary have apparently forgotten about that, or they know nothing about it.
May 14, 1982

A businessman called me the other day. He had a German-made loader on which he broke the hose. It was a metric hose. He bought a Canadian-made hose, the same size, drove 50 miles, and took it back because it would not fit.
I would be the last person in the world to stop a universal system, Mr. Speaker. In fact, I would have thought that, had the government any imagination whatsoever, that is the type of system we would be moving to. But we are not; we have a worse system today than we ever had. I just happen to have half a dozen nuts and bolts here, and this is what it is all about, Mr. Speaker. I know I am not supposed to display anything, but here they are if anyone wants to see them. None of them will fit. In the agriculture industry it used to be that you had your two styles and the measurements were always the same: 1/2; 3/4; 7/8; 3/16; or whatever it is. They were all the same. You could guarantee that a coarse thread of any size would fit, the same with a fine thread. And here these are, and none of them fit. This is the problem we are running into. I am told there are up to 15 different sizes in bolts, so it means that you can no longer go by size, you have to go by parts. Can you imagine what that will mean to the business community, to farmers? No longer can they rely on what we have called the Imperial measurement.
We have been ridiculed this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, because Sir John A. Macdonald allowed two systems of measurement. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, Canada came a long way with the two systems side by side in 110 years. I learned metric when I went to school, and there was no problem. I learned the Imperial system. They worked together and that is the way it has been. And all this garbage which has been presented to us today is absolutely unbelievable. They read a statement from the President of the United States. Well, what has happened in the U.S.? The U.S. Metric Board has been told by the Reagan administration to walk their last kilometre. Their transportation department floated a plan for switching highway signs from miles to kilometres, but an outcry from Congress prevented it from reaching the board for official consideration. The same for a plan by the national weather service to determine temperatures exclusively in Celsius instead of Fahrenheit. That metric weather plan never reached the board for consideration, and is dormant.
We just heard that the provinces were full partners in this plan. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think it was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who misled the premiers of our provinces. I remember in 1976, when one of the provinces made a move towards metrication, I asked a member of that legislature why they did it. He said that the Prime Minister said it was inevitable and that all of Canada was going that way. He misled them. Now we find the provinces backing out. Just this week Nova Scotia, unanimously-I suppose that takes in some Liberal members, if they have any-moved a resolution to opt out of forced metric. For them to stand up in this House and say that the provinces are full partners, well, 1 have never heard anything so ridiculous and dishonest in my life.
The minister says he is going to assist any hardship cases. Is he prepared to assist the broadloom company in Montreal which has a chain of, I think, seven stores? They have gone
Supply
bankrupt, and they have now been fined $1,700 for not complying with the government's order in council, its edict on forced metrication. Is the minister prepared to assist the woman in Calgary who appeared before a court not so many days ago because she was advertising her product in metric and Imperial side by side so that she would be taking advantage? A representative of the minister's department went into her store and laid a charge, so is the minister prepared to assist her? Is that what our charter of rights means? We have this kind of thing happening to some of our people before the ink on the charter is even dry. Where is the freedom in this country? I guess possibly one of the problems which has befallen us as Conservatives is that in 1975-76 we trusted that government to keep its word.
Reference has been made time and time again to the white paper Ged Baldwin agreed to. Yes, Ged Baldwin agreed to a voluntary system of weights and measurements, nothing more! That is what we agreed to in 1975-76. There was not a vote on that omnibus bill when it went through-and this is why I have argued with members opposite-because we were not happy with it. The government had a majority. We made a deal with the government that if it put back the measurement of acres in the bill relating to the Canadian Wheat Board and left the system voluntary, we would not oppose it by a vote even though we had held up the bill for months. The government wanted that bill. There was a further understanding with respect to that, which was that we would keep in step with the United States.
We are told that we are going into metric to facilitate our trade. But 75 per cent of our trade is with the United States. How utterly ridiculous that is. I have seven or eight documents here which show that Canadian companies are making deals with their United States counterpats and there is money coming into Canada for deals all made in Imperial measurement. My friend, the hon. member for Regina West, said that he was out to Bombardier, and the U.S. wanted the LRC in metric. They only take it in metric because that is the way it is set up. But the hon. member never said anything about Cana-dair, did he, Mr. Speaker? He never said anything about Canadair at all. Canadair tried to go metric but it could not. Other facets of the air industry have tried to go metric but they cannot do it. Why does the government take the small corner grocery stores across our country and enforce metric measurement on them? There are certain areas where metric conversion is unenforceable. Why do hon. members opposite not talk to representatives of the lumber industry in British Columbia? I talked to a member of that industry the other day. He told me that the only orders he has in metric are from the federal government. He told me that all sales to the United States are in the Imperial measurement. The largest order ever from Japan for prefab homes is in the Imperial measurement. Why in the world does the government lay on the heavy hand and force people into something that is unnecessary? People

May 14, 1982
Supply
should not have to convert to metric, quite apart from the fact that it is very costly to do so.
Today I asked the minister a question. He almost jeered at me as if I were creating problems. That question is very relevant in western Canada because it has to do with the beef farmer and the beef industry, which industry is one of the greater providers of income in Alberta. I want to read a portion of a letter written to me from Mr. Ralph Void who speaks on behalf of the beef farmers. This letter is dated September 1, 1981. In part his letter reads:
This photostat tells the story January 1, 1984. Could we not have another election before this?
I do not suppose we will. Mr. Void enclosed a photocopy of a document to which he was referring. His letter also stated:
I have been in Ottawa three times and Winnipeg twice over metric.
Mr. Void made five trips to Winnipeg and to Ottawa in an attempt to impress upon the government that it should not be moving to convert the beef industry to metric. But now a brown envelope has shown up mysteriously stating that the government intends to force metric in the beef industry on January 21, 1984. That is not fair. It is not just and it is not in the best interests of the livestock industry. The argument is used that it is being done for trade. Goodness me, anyone who knows anything about trade in the beef industry recognizes that the greatest amount of trade is with our neighbour to the south, the United States. The buyers of our purebred cattle come up here to sales and shows. I do not suppose anybody opposite, not even the member for Regina West, has ever been to a livestock show, otherwise he would know that in front of each animal is the date of birth and the rate of weight gain. The hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield) understands this. The rate of gain is very important. The pounds per day gain is what they recognize in the United States. But now the Americans will come up here and will have to figure out everything in kilograms. Of course, the same situation will occur when animals are sold at auction. I do not know how many members opposite have ever been to a cattle auction. I doubt whether the minister himself has ever been inside an auction mart. At these auctions, split second decisions have to be made in the purchase of large numbers of cattle. As I say, trade goes back and forth across the border. It is a very healthy industry and it is a healthy way to do business. But all that will have to change. Canadians are going to be forced into a different system than the one followed in the United States.
As time goes on, and perhaps if this government is successful in what it is trying to do, it will mean that our young people who are growing up today, will know nothing about the system that is being used in the United States. That, to me, is a crazy way of doing things. I am sure our young people going to school today are just as intelligent as we were when we were going to school and we had the two systems.
The government is trying to push two languages. Therefore, why can we not have two systems of weights and measures? It seems to me that before we have two language systems, it would be far better for us to have two systems of weights and measures which have stood us in good stead for well over 100
years. The government is wrong. It is dead wrong going in that direction. The only sensible thing to do, as the hon. member for Regina West said, was for the government to allow industries or businesses to go to the system best suited to their interests, and let them convert to metric in their own time. But here we have a government that is prepared to throw people in jail. This government is prepared to fine people up to $5,000 if they do not comply with the edicts of this government.
There has never been a time in Canadian history when the Canadian people distrusted a government as much as they distrust this one, and I will tell you why. First, there was the War Measures Act, which was the start of it all. Second came wage and price controls. Third, the government told Canadians that energy prices should not go up too drastically. But look at what has happened. Three times now we have heard the people say, "That is enough." And it is a reason, in spite of what the minister says, for the majority of Canadians to tell us they do not want the metric system enforced upon them at this time. There is absolutely no way that Canadians are prepared to accept that edict. If the minister thinks he is right, why does he not have a plebiscite on the matter and give the people a chance to voice their opinion? If the minister were really honest in the approach he is taking, he would disband temporarily the Metric Commission. He could wait for the next election, which will probably come in a year or two. We have lived 110 years with the two systems side by side. Why can we not live for another two years with it? Let us have a plebiscite at the same time as the next election. Let the people vote on whether or not they want to convert to metric. I am sure if the majority of Canadians wanted the metric system, the minority would go along with them. But the majority is not prepared to accept the edict of this government.
We have just had a provincial by-election in my constituency in western Canada. I am sure that members opposite are pretty much aware of the results of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: You lost.

One of the main platforms on which that candidate was elected was anti-metric. He garnered more votes than all other candidates put together. The minister then tells me that a majority of the people favour the metric system. How is it then that that candidate won an election on that issue with over 50 per cent of the vote?
Some of the things the minister has been saying are absolutely untrue. The government's approach to metrication is callous, brutal, insensitive, and it is an underhanded method. It is unfortunate that it is being imposed upon Canadians by order in council, the refuge of the scoundrel. The government does not have the courage or the courtesy to permit Canadians to have laws which affect their lives and their livelihood discussed in open debate in the House. Again, it governs by stealth through jackboot tactics. I protest the brown shirt method of circumventing parliamentary debate through the use of order in council to impose metrication, make imperial
May 14, 1982

illegal and set up a system of fines or imprisonment for those Canadians who prefer to engage in business and commerce in Imperial or in both systems.
For the benefit of the minister who said that perhaps we have been reading some of these stories, Mrs. Kasparian told me this morning, after quite a lengthy discussion, that she is quite prepared to go to jail before she will change her mind or pay a fine.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to this motion which requests a moratorium on the implementation of a planned metric conversion program in Canada.
As my friend, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin) mentioned earlier, he was not in the House when the idea and the approval was given for converting to the metric system. I, too, was not here.
However, I have been involved in the media and broadcasting industry over the years and recall doing a number of special programs relating to the conversion to the metric system on a number of occasions. It is because of that experience that I wanted to have an opportunity to speak this afternoon.
Based on some past records and information, I think it is very necessary that we set the record straight with facts and figures since all we have heard throughout this entire metric debate-especially from the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) and some of his colleagues-has been nothing but scare tactics. We heard about scare tactics from the last speaker, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) when he talked about fines and imprisonment and created the impression that everyone opposed to metric will go to jail. That is the furthest thing from the truth. I believe any sensible Canadian knows that. It is nothing but scare tactics on the part of the opposition.
The Official Opposition.
The only opposition.

It is really very little opposition today. For example, when we think of the concerns about the beef industry, I would remind the House that the chairman of the Metric Commission, Mr. McArthur, comes from the city of Calgary and is a retired businessman. Also, the executive director of the Metric Commission, Mr. Beckman, is also from Alberta and previously was a civil servant in the provincial government. I am sure that these two gentlemen will have the very best interests of the beef farmer in mind when it comes to implementing the metric system. I am sure that the beef farmers, not only in western Canada but throughout all of Canada, will be well served just by the fact that we have these two men in place operating the Metric Commission in our country.
The debate so far as been very emotional. As I mentioned earlier, I would like to put on the record some of the events which have taken place in a very quiet and orderly manner. It is very easy to rant and rave and present scare tactics, as we
Supply
have heard this afternoon. It is another matter to conduct proper research and come up with the proper facts and figures. Therefore, I would like to mention some of those facts officially for the record.
First, I will describe the nature of the national conversion program as it now exists. As has already been mentioned this afternoon, over 100 sectors are operating within the framework of the Metric Commission of Canada and represent all areas of endeavor ranging from iron and steel mills to fishing and farming. Of course, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie is well aware of what is happening in the iron and steel mills.
Of these 100 sectors, only three-gasoline sales by the litre, home furnishings and retail food scales-are subject to regulations under the Weights and Measures Act of 1976-77. Both of these Acts were fully debated over many months and Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada was requested by the industries involved to make relevant regulation changes in support of the conversion to the metric system. Not only were these regulation changes supported by industry, they were also endorsed by the Consumers Association of Canada. The remaining sectors are converting according to time tables as suggested by over 2,000 industry volunteers in every sector of the Canadian economy. In order to facilitate the implementation of sector plans, existing measurement sensitive regulations and legislation must be converted to metric units at some point in the program. In this respect there are three main industries where regulations under the federal Weights and Measures Act are restrictive with respect to measurement units. They are the three which I mentioned earlier: gasoline dispensing, home furnishings and retail food sales.
Metric Commission Canada has established planning methods and scheduling procedures based on industry consensus for the renewal and approval of the sector plans which are national in their scope and application.
The planning methodology established by the commission for use of voluntary-I stress the word "voluntary"-sector committees offers the means of change, and the actual implementation is initiated in co-operation with the specified business or industrial sector.
I would like to mention in greater detail each of the three conversion programs where it had been considered necessary to publish regulations under the Weights and Measures Act. I wish to do so in order to dispel the notion that metric conversion is being implemented in Canada by legislative compulsion in the face of overwhelming resistance from business, industry, education, labour and consumer organizations.
With respect to the conversion to gasoline sales by the litre and the conversion of other petroleum products, an ad hoc committee comprised of representatives from the major Canadian petroleum companies first met in July, 1972-ten years ago-to assess the opportunities and problems facing the industry with respect to metric conversion. One year later the group agreed to the formation of a committee covering petroleum refineries, wholesalers and gasoline service stations for the purpose of developing a suitable conversion plan and

This sector has a major economic impact on the Canadian economy. Petroleum products with which we are familiar and which are refined and marketed in Canada include gasoline, fuel oils, lubricating and illuminating oils, greases and petrochemical agricultural products. During 1976, some remote areas of the country were faced with gasoline prices in excess of $1 per gallon. I am sure many members will remember that the response by the industry was to introduce half-gallon pricing, since pump price dials could not be set at a price greater than 99.9 cents per gallon. At the same time, Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada was urging the industry to minimize half-gallon pricing. A bulletin put out by CCAC in 1976 limited the duration of half-gallon pricing to 12 months. As a result, the sector's pump conversion task force examined the feasibility of converting service station pumps to dispensing in litres. Alternatives to metric conversion were considered but none were viable.
The sector committee persuaded CCAC to rescind its bulletin limiting half-gallon pricing on the understanding that the industry was committed to the eventual conversion of service station pumps to litre dispensing. In preparation for conversion, new pumps were being ordered beginning in late 1975 with supplementary metric gear boxes installed which could be activated later so as to operate in the litre mode.
The sector's metric conversion plan called for conversion to commence on January 1, 1979, and be essentially complete in two years' time. However, both the industry and CCAC were concerned with a possible haphazard conversion of pumps to metric. Thus, regulations were drafted by CCAC in concert with the sector committee, so that pump conversion could begin on January 1, 1979 and, with certain exceptions, be complete by December 31, 1980. The exceptions referred to small retail outlets in remote regions dispensing less than 100,000 gallons per year. The conversion of retail pumps began on schedule and implementation is complete at this time except in some sparsely populated regions. Virtually no complaints were received concerning the program, making it a "non-event" in terms of consumer reaction.
Aside from the conversion of retail gasoline pumps, the provincial tax acts for petroleum products had to be converted. As we know, all provinces now have litre taxes. Perhaps one of the most difficult areas in the program which required considerable lead time was the conversion of the many measurement-sensitive business systems used by each company.
The use of regulations under the Weights and Measures Act was also requested by the home furnishings industry. The minister referred to this earlier today. A notice was published in the Canada Gazette, Part I, on March 17, 1979 by Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada to issue regulations under the Weights and Measures Act regarding this industry. The proposed regulations established cut-off dates after which the advertising, offering for sale or sale of piece goods and home
furnishings in other than the international metric system of units would be illegal. The products involved include linens, beddings, furniture, carpets, wallpaper and resilient flooring. The request for regulations was initiated by a subcommittee on home furnishings of the sector committee for consumers, home economics and retail trade. The recommendation was supported by the full sector committee and other committees for textiles, wood, furniture, paper and allied products, and labour.

The committee on home furnishings decided it would be in the best interests of the consumer to plan for metric conversion to take place in all of their areas at the same time. This decision was based on a reasonable assumption that someone buying carpeting would likely be wanting to look at furniture, bedspreads and wallpaper at the same time. It was thought that it would be only confusing for the consumer to have to buy one of these products in customary units and another in metric units. It was also felt that because of the competitive nature of their own industry, regulations would be required to ensure that all retailers converted at the same time. Just on that point, the hon. member for Red Deer mentioned a carpet company which had gone out of business in the Montreal area, I believe. The courts are now charged with the matter. It may come as a surprise to many hon. members of the House that an example of one of the many low profile sectors converting to metric, without fanfare and on a strictly voluntary basis, is the fire-fighting equipment and operation sector, which is a very important sector to our way of life and to our protection as Canadian citizens. This sector includes equipment manufacturers and distributors as well as the fire protection and fire fighting services across Canada. Several major associations and government bodies when contacted in October, 1977 expressed considerable enthusiasm in forming a sector committee to determine their interest in metric conversion.
Associations which are represented include the Canadian Fire Apparatus Manufacturers Association, the Fire Equipment Manufacturers Institute, the International and Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs and the Association of Canadian Fire Marshalls and Fire Commissioners. Standards writing organizations such as Underwriters Laboratories and the National Fire Protection Association are also represented. The economic impact of this sector is mainly associated with the supplies, equipment and capital facilities which are used by the fire protection and firefighting services. The major emphasis concerns safety and the establishment of effective operational services, yet we have all these organizations, the firefighting community, in line with metric conversion. We know the principal benefits expected from metric conversion in this sector concerning the economy and safety enhancement that can be realized from the standardization of many types of equipment.

These organizations were convinced and are convinced of the practical benefits to be derived from a system whose advantages range from simplifying the learning process in school to improving and consolidating Canada's competitive position in world trade.
There are over 100 voluntary sector committees with over 2,000 volunteer representatives from industry, labour, consumer and government bodies. Metric Commission Canada initiated the over-all strategy of involving every sector from every region of Canada as early as possible in planning for metric conversion. Does that sound very compulsory, Mr. Speaker?
Sector plans of industry, business and education are developed through a consensus process. Voluntary sector committees take responsibility for scheduling and monitoring the implementation of their plans. The voluntary participation approach is characterized by plans which are developed by those who will have to implement them. This helps to ensure that the benefits are achieved at minimal cost.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, to delay and prolong the implementation of metric simply increases the cost. That is about the only thing it accomplishes, and that is negative.
A program of guideline dates for metric conversion recommended by Metric Commission Canada, after consulting with industry, labour and consumer groups, was approved by the government and debated in the House of Commons on March 17, 1975. The standing committee reported back to the House on December 17, 1976, with recommendations to adopt the program of guideline dates and to introduce additional legislation supporting metric conversion.
That bill was debated in the House, it went to committee and after eight months was reported back to the House with recommendations for legislation regarding the implementation of metric conversion, but still the opposition goes about the country saying it has never been debated in Parliament; that it is being forced down people's throats; that Parliament has not been consulted and therefore the people have not been consulted. That is a lot of nonsense, Mr. Speaker, and it is time they
stopped using that kind of scare tactic and started using logic. Surely hon. members opposite must have heard something before now about the necessity of elected representatives of the people providing leadership. Maybe it is time that some of them started providing a little of that leadership and began explaining the facts instead of exacerbating the situation and promoting the canards that they spread across the country about the metric system as well as many other aspects of government policy.
Out of a total of 94 sectors which have public conversion plans there are only three sectors for which regulations have been issued under the Weights and Measures Act. These regulations establish cutoff dates for the sale and advertising of goods in other than the metric SI system. Regulations were requested by the working group on scales in the retail food industry, by the home furnishing and piece goods industry, by the petroleum refiners and by the wholesale and gasoline service stations. These committees have consumer, industry and appropriate government representation on them. Proposals to make metric conversion mandatory in these three industries were initiated by the industries concerned and not by Metric Commission Canada. Where regulatory action has been requested, the industries cited were concerned about achieving an orderly conversion without unfair competition. Government action was requested to ensure that the ground rules for metric conversion are the same for all in the industry, thus reducing the possibility of consumer confusion to a minimum. The Consumers' Association of Canada approved this approach.
The working group on scales in the retail food industry comprises representatives of food retailing chains and independents, scales manufacturing and servicing enterprises, consumers and weights and measures regulating authorities. In 1977 it formally requested suitable regulations under the Weights and Measures Act to deal with advertising as well as the conversion of scales, which were deemed necessary for achieving a co-ordinated and orderly transition to metric units. I wish to emphasize the fact that the decision to support mandatory metric conversion in this sector was made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and the cabinet under the authority of the statute law on the recommendation of the food retailers in 1977, and with the full support of the Consumers' Association of Canada.
The information I have provided in my remarks so far, Mr. Speaker, indicates that the Canadian metric conversion program has followed a voluntary participation approach. Where legislation has been enacted and regulations used, it has been at the request of the interested parties.
I would also like to remind hon. members that this program is now in its tenth year and is approaching completion in many significant areas. Several sectors within the Metric Commission Canada framework have already identified to the commission that implementation of metric conversion in their industries is now substantially complete. Based on the 94 conversion

plans currently published by Canadian business, industry, education, labour, farm, consumer and other sectors, about 80 per cent of these sectors expect to achieve their completion goals before December, 1984. In addition, the conversion of scales in retail food stores, which is the last major program to affect consumers, is now under way in the major urban centres across Canada. Consequently, I suggest this is not a time for seeking a review of our metric conversion policy. If we have a review now and change horses this late when we are almost to the other shore, what is it going to do to all of those industries which have already converted? The opposition is worrying about costs, yet they want us to turn the hands of the clock backwards. Sometimes I wonder how many of them over there have accepted the wrist watch yet.
The reason given for the introduction of the Weights and Measures Act in 1871 was:
It is expedient to legalize the use of the metric system of weights and measures for the promotion and extension of the internal as well as the foreign trade of Canada, and for the advancement of science.
One hundred years later, in January, 1970 the white paper on metric conversion in Canada stated:
Because of the vital importance of foreign trade to Canada, especially the need for growth in exports of manufactured goods, there must be serious concern about Canada's competitiveness in world markets as a result of the worldwide changeover to the metric system.
It went on to say that:
Since a trading nation must take account of the measurement and standards system of the buyer, the overwhelming world trend to the metric system is a powerful argument for Canadian conversion.
The government fully anticipated that adoption of the metric system would improve Canada's ability to penetrate world markets with manufactured goods, and that holds true today.
We heard about the United States, and the U.S. ambassador to Canada has a penchant for shooting off his mouth, saying that conversion to metric would hurt Canadian trade with the U.S.
I just want to close, Mr. Speaker, by saying that about 50 per cent of all exports to the U.S. today are in metric measure. Therefore, it has not hurt our exports, it is not likely to, and despite the reactionary regime in the U.S. at the moment, they too will convert to metric.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to be able to say a few words on this subject. I am also delighted to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) here; I am aware he has stayed for pretty well the entire time of the debate. However, there is one thing he did not mention in his very kind offer to the people of Canada, so I will do it for him. Some few days ago the minister stated that he would be delighted to hear from all the people in Canada on metric and he would answer them all personally. I think the invitation still holds, and I hope those in favour will write to the minister as well. I also hope he will give us the results some weeks or months down the road.
Supply
There is one other thing which is very unusual, Mr. Speaker, and this is why I feel the minister is very concerned about this motion. The minister spoke for 35 minutes outlining his case. Being a very distinguished Member of Parliament and cabinet from the province of Quebec, it is the only time he never said one word in French. He was trying to get the message across to that part of Canada which is not so enthusiastic about this program. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am going to go a little further than the minister and say, "Bienvenue a mon collegue." So I have spoken more in French than the minister has.
The motion before us today, Mr. Speaker, is on a very specific issue, one which a great many Canadians feel is of singular importance, and I appreciate the privilege of being able to speak on their behalf. As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that in our Press Gallery today is a very distinguished former parliamentarian in the person of the former Leader of the Social Credit Party, Mr. Robert Thompson.
Hear, hear!

He is also a former Conservative MP. I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps the truly significant aspect of the debate on this issue is the fact that the necessity for such debate reflects upon and embodies something absolutely fundamental to each and every issue debated in this chamber. I am referring to democracy, appropriately defined as government by the people, direct or representative. We on both sides of this chamber are here because we are part of democracy. The people of Canada elect us to represent their views and act in their interest. This is the way democracy works in Canada, or at least this is the way it is supposed to work. However, under this government, and increasingly evident during all debates in this House, government by the people-democracy-has all but been abandoned in many cases. The views of the people we represent and our capability to act in their interest have been swept aside and dismissed by the authoritative and arrogant attitude of the government. Our treasured form of democracy is being replaced by a form of tyranny, which is described as "a despotic and cruel exercise of power".
That this government is both despotic and cruel is something well known to the thousands of unemployed, homeless and hungry Canadians. Its despotic and cruel exercise of power has destroyed our economy. As I mentioned some time ago, the indifference of this government is such that, having shattered the economic base of the nation, its only response to victimized Canadians is that they must adjust to living amidst the rubble. Recently, and with increasing regularity, the victims of this tyranny are registering their refusal to adjust. As this becomes evident, Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be most appropriate at this time to quote the remarks of someone who obviously neglected to heed his own warnings:
The great lesson to draw from revolutions is not that they devour humanity, but rather that tyranny never fails to generate them.

May 14, 1982
Supply
The words I have just quoted were written in 1958. The author, 24 years later, has become universally viewed as a very despotic Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). As the Prime Minister said, tyranny never fails to generate revolution. Among the many growing forms of protest we are witnessing against this government is one which involves the issue we debate today, namely, the mandatory conversion to metric measurement. Let me repeat that, "the mandatory conversion".
The motion before us bears repeating because it so clearly exemplifies the importance not only of the motion but of the debate itself. It is that the compulsory element in metrication should and must be abandoned as an affront to representative, parliamentary democracy.
To compel Canadians, to order them, to convert to the metric system or be punished is abhorrent and odious. When this tyrannical method of conversion is so obviously against the wishes of the majority of the people so compelled, it is indeed an affront to democracy.
There can be no doubt in the mind of the government that the majority of people in this country are against being forced into metric conversion. This government knows that various public opinion polls have impartially tabulated this opposition. Members on both sides of this House have received letters from constituents registering strong objection.
Just over a month ago, I and a number of my colleagues on this side of the House presented to the House a massive petition opposing the mandatory method of conversion, a petition bearing some 130,000 signatures. The names on this petition were collected for the most part in response to a mail-in poll conducted by the Sun newspapers in Toronto, Calgary and Edmonton. Canadians in three major centres of this nation took the time to express their disapproval in this way. Almost as significant as the fact that so many people felt strongly enough opposed to being forced into using metric that they participated in the poll is the fact they had to spend 30 cents on a stamp to reply. That means Michael Warren, the Postmaster General, and his post office gain to the tune of about $40,000. No one in this House need be reminded that the decision to raise our postal rates was not made by, nor even referred to, Parliament.
Let me repeat for the benefit of viewers and those listening and reading my remarks that when they write regarding postal matters to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs they can write to him free of postal charge. He will still have to spend his time opening and replying to those letters. The rise in postal rates is one glaring example of what this government has done to extract a considerable amount of money from the taxpayers much against their will. This rise in rates, like the compulsory nature of the switch to metric, was passed by a government order in council, both evidence of despotic and cruel exercise of power.
The government, in its devious attempts to confuse the issue with respect to parliamentary approval and input into the
switch to metric, cites, with glaring omissions, past approval of opposition parties. The government knows full well that what it is saying about this aspect of conversion and what really occurred are two completely different things.
Back in 1971 when the Progressive Conservative opposition agreed to support the government's white paper on metric conversion, our support was based, among others, on two main considerations. At that time it appeared that other nations, notably our major trading partners, were also going to convert to the system, and it made sense to keep in step with the times. The government, in its white paper, drew attention to this fact. At that time I had the privilege of speaking, not only inside but outside of the House on the subject. I said that I could see some merit in moving toward metric on the basis that our biggest trading partner, the United States, was going that way. I said that we should move at the same speed as the United States, and you know what that is now. We find in the white paper the following:
-because of the close ties between the United States and Canada in science, technology, industry and commerce, each country has a special interest in the course likely to be followed by the other in respect of metric conversion.
The government assured us that Canada would co-ordinate her conversion with that of the United States. From that I gather it meant at the same speed. Since then, as a result of strong public opposition, the United States has backed away from the process and is abolishing its Metric Board and placing the question of conversion under the aegis of the department of commerce to pursue voluntary conversion if desired.
Our other trading partners, Britain and Japan, have also either halted the conversion process or are reverting to the voluntary system, again as a result of strong opposition from the public. Only in Canada, what a pity-that reminds me of the tea ad we see on television when we hear "Only in Canada, you say. What a pity!"-do we have the spectre of people being fined or imprisoned if they do not comply. Only in Canada has tyranny replaced democracy.
The second major consideration which led to our support of the white paper was that one section of the paper stated:
No legislative action is contemplated which would make mandatory a general use of metric.
Would the government now have us believe that the order in council making metric conversion mandatory is "no legislative action"? That is yet another broken promise by a government which has perfected the process of saying one thing and then doing exactly the opposite. The government knows and has always known that Canadians are firmly opposed to mandatory metric conversion.
The first evidence of this arose in 1977 when western farmers and Members of Parliament forced the government to amend the metric conversion bill to enable grain producers to keep the acre as the major unit of land measurement. The bill was also amended to allow the natural gas industry to sell gas either in cubic feet, cubic metres or other forms of measurement depending on whether gas was sold by volume, mass or
May 14, 1982

energy units. At the time the fight was won a western newspaper noted that when it came to domestic usage, the retention of the imperial system of measurement "would hinder nobody except the Ottawa bureaucrats determined to hammer us all into neat moulds of conformism."
Another example of the problems faced by Canadians in dealing with metric conversion occurred the year after the farmers won their battle. The year 1978 was to be the primary conversion year in Canada for the construction industry. Problems surfaced almost as soon as the program began. Millions of homes in the country were built according to imperial measurement, and the maintenance and upkeep of these houses required supplies conforming to the same system. Manufacturers faced the cost of double production lines and suppliers faced the cost of stocking two inventories, one metric, the other imperial.
Thousands upon thousands of self-employed Canadians, carpenters, plumbers, carpet layers and the like faced horrendous costs to covert their tools, all because of the government's incomprehensible and unwavering march toward total metrication.
It was in October of that same year that the comptroller-general's report to the United States Congress was published. The report estimated that metric conversion would cost the United States about $100 billion and, after dealing at length with each aspect of a potential change-over, warned Americans that the metric system might not be that great a deal after all. Usually in Canada we hear it said that it would be one tenth of the cost. You can imagine what it would be. We have heard figures given by government spokesmen that it is just a few million dollars. The only great deal involved in the Canadian conversion program is the great deal of money that it will cost us. It will be astronomical. It will be extremely difficult to put any figure on it. This year's budget for the Canadian Metric Commission is $12 million, and of this amount $1.8 million will be spent on advertising. The total cost of the commission's budget, since it was formed in 1972, is now $50 million, and in all probability a good deal more than that is hidden in other estimates and in other departments.
But the Canadian government continues its quest, still holding firm to the belief that mandatory conversion is absolutely necessary because metric measurement is the greatest thing to have happened to improve our lives since the advent of sliced bread. That is probably why the government took its toughest stance on metric in the area of retail food sales.
Here, as well, Canadians are and will be paying through the nose because of the way the government approached the issue.
With conversion dates firm and fixed, retailers had no choice but to replace or adjust the more than 120,000 food scales in Canadian food stores, outlets both large and small.
The cost to the retailers has been accurately estimated to be between $2,000 and $8,000. Yet the minister in his remarks earlier today, stated that it was a few hundred dollars. What I

find equally ludicrous is the fact that 98 per cent of all new metric food scales in Canada are manufactured outside of Canada. Over one half billion dollars is being spent outside of Canada to implement a program that we do not even want here, or at least the majority do not want.
If our grocery vendors refuse to comply with the rules of the government's mandatory metric conversion program and decide that the unnecessary cost to them and the inconvenience and annoyance to their customers is not worth it, they can be fined up to $5,000 or jailed for up to two years. The minister did budge somewhat when he said that he might consider small retailers being exempt. We wonder just how small a retailer will have to be in order to be exempt.
This plan to punish retailers for non-compliance may be one of the reasons why the government proclaimed yet another order in council-the Emergency Measures Act. It might be planning to incarcerate grocery store owners in the civilian internment camps it plans to establish.
Come on, do not say that.

Come on, it is there. It is very unlikely but it is there.
I might also remind the government that when our party was in office we recognized the folly of the retail sales program, and the minister then responsible for small business, the member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), cancelled the order in council at the request of the retail food sector.
However, once again under this government, the metric juggernaut rolls blindly along. It is a government uncaring that the sacrifices being made by those in its path are forced to adopt the metric measurement and being ordered to comply. In a great many areas of our life metric has become a fait accompli but not because, as the government would have us believe, it is advantageous either to the individual or the nation.
Metric measurement of our gasoline has certainly not led to a lowering of prices. Metric measurement of highway speed limits has certainly not resulted in fewer accidents. Metric measurement of consumer products has certainly not expanded our overseas trade opportunities. Metric measurement of our environment has certainly not helped eliminate the menace of acid rain. Metric measurement of the tools of labour is certainly not stemming the tide of unemployment. Metric measurement of the distance from home plate to the outfield fence in Olympic Stadium has certainly not guaranteed Expo fans that the Montreal Expos will win the World Series. If the minister has ever seen that field on television, the distances are shown in huge numbers in metric and much smaller ones in feet. You need field glasses to see them.
Metric measurement of our meat and produce certainly will not save families money on their grocery bill. It is, rather, the opposite. Every time metric is used it seems that the goods that are purchased cost more.

Mr. Speaker, since we have only five minutes left, I think I will have the privilege of ending this debate. First, I would like to say in passing that if the member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) is paying $23 or $24 per gallon, he is not buying it at the right place, because I pay $18. So, better luck next year.
Substantially, what does the motion say, Mr. Speaker? The member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) is asking to abandon metrication forthwith. In fact, the position taken by the members opposite has become a real farce. I have never heard Progressive Conservative members give so many different opinions on a given subject. In any case, it was the same for Petro-Canada, the interest rates we are discussing currently and the Constitution. The metric system is no exception. What was their position in 1979? They favoured conversion to the metric system as soon as possible. The then Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was asked the following question by my colleague, the member for Timmins-Chapleau, and I quote:
I would like to ask the minister how he intends to ensure that metric conversion is completed, or does he intend to act on his own to dismantle the program?
He answered, and I quote:
Certainly not, Mr. Speaker. The government is still committed to the concept of metrication.
I also want to quote a question by the member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), which was reported in Hansard of
November 14, 1979, page 1302, and directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and I quote:
Therefore, I want to give him an opportunity to correct an impression that he gave yesterday when he is quoted as having said there is a possibility that there will be a postponement of the conversion to the metric system, planned for January 1-
And the then Minister of State responsible for Small Businesses and Industry answered, and I quote:
The fact is, the whole process has been handled very well by the members of the Metric Commission, who are engineers, who have been dealing with sectors of industry and associations, who have had time to sit down and study the various implications and problems involved.
Going back a little further, to March 1975 when they were the official opposition, my hon. colleague, the member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), the Progressive Conservative whip, made an excellent speech. He spoke on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party, and I am referring to what was reported in Hansard on March 17, 1975, on page 4060, and I quote:
I am pleased to lead off this debate for the official opposition. I think 1 should say at the outset that we supported metric conversion when it was introduced by order in council and the white paper, and that is our position today: we still support it. Let me say again that we in the official opposition support the principle of metric conversion.
And the hon. member, who today is the Progressive Conservative Party whip, went on to say, and I quote:
-the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was prime minister, had his ministers undertake studies in this field.
So I would ask the hon. members representing the Progressive Conservative Party to contradict the right hon. former member for Prince Albert.
The member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) said that he never voted on the issue. 1 would refer him to Hansard, June 16, 1977, page 1142, on the subject of Bill C-23, where it says that the member for Red Deer voted on that day on Bill C-23, introduced by this government.
